sentences:
OfBusiness is heading for the stock market with a business that earns most of its revenue in one place and most of its profits in another
The imbalance raises a larger question.
Can OfBusiness improve the returns on its commerce business while using lending and technology to earn more from each SME relationship?

Here’s how the business makes money, and where its economics are changing
OfBusiness is heading for the stock market with a business that earns most of its revenue in one place and most of its profits in another.
Commerce, which spans raw-material trading, manufacturing and apparel, brings in almost all its sales.
Yet its lending business, led by Oxyzo, contributes more than half its segment profits despite being a fraction of commerce’s size.
Ahead of the IPO, the question is whether commerce can earn more from its scale, or whether lending will keep carrying the profits.
The startup began its journey by helping small and medium enterprises buy raw materials and access working capital.

Over the past decade, it has gone from sourcing steel and chemicals for manufacturers to making some of those products itself, expanding into apparel and building a sizable lending business through Oxyzo.
Along the way, it has achieved something relatively rare in India’s B2B commerce sector.
Not only has OfBusiness built a ₹20,000 Cr-plus profitable business, but both the company and its lending arm Oxyzo have independently achieved unicorn status.
That’s a notable contrast with B2B commerce peers such as Udaan, Moglix and Zetwerk, which have struggled with losses.
Infra.Market is another exception, having reported ₹220 Cr in net profit on ₹18,472 Cr in revenue in FY25.
But as the company prepares for its stock market debut, its FY26 financials reveal an interesting shift.
Consolidated operating revenue declined nearly 8% year on year, even as net profit climbed 21% to ₹724 Cr.

One business is key on revenue and another on balance sheet with both contributing to ~50% of profits
Commerce, which includes raw-material trading and manufacturing, generated 93% of OfBusiness’ ₹20,472 Cr consolidated operating revenue in FY26.
Yet financial services, led by Oxyzo, accounted for more than half its segment pre-tax profits.
The lending-led business generated ₹505 Cr in profit before tax, compared with ₹422 Cr from commerce.

Considering the varying nature of the commerce and lending business, the key question is if OfBusiness can simultaneously deliver growth in returns on its commerce business along with the lending business as both scale.
The answer lies in how its procurement, manufacturing, customer-discovery and financing operations work together.
Here’s how the business makes money, and where its economics are changing.
OfBusiness’ commerce business runs on three layers: raw-material trading, manufacturing and finished goods.
Trading brings scale, manufacturing helps improve margins, and finished goods open up new markets.
The first layer is straightforward.
OfBusiness aggregates demand from manufacturers, sources materials and manages pricing, quality and delivery.
More than 12,000 SMEs and emerging corporates transacted on OfCommerce in FY26, across a catalogue of 103 products.
These services give the group a way to reach SMEs before they need procurement or credit; neither platform’s standalone revenue is disclosed.
But there’s a limitation to this model.
Commodity trading is a high-volume, low-margin business, and fluctuations in prices can quickly affect revenue.
Owing to exit of some the low-return products, Metals, OfBusiness’ largest category, saw sales decline 20% to ₹10,434 Cr.
Chemicals grew just 4% to ₹3,663 Cr, while food processing and other products fell 55% to ₹1,636 Cr.
Part of the contraction was strategic.
OfBusiness said it exited lower-return commerce categories and discontinued operations to prioritise margins and manufacturing integration.
But the shareholder letter also cites lower mild-steel prices and delays in two mega projects.
The disclosures do not isolate how much of the metal’s decline came from deliberate exits versus these headwinds.
The second layer, manufacturing, is OfBusiness’ attempt to improve these economics.

As cofounder Asish Mohapatra said in September 2026, “As these ecosystems deepen, we are building manufacturing capabilities selectively in categories where we see an opportunity to add value to the supply chain.”
Instead of simply buying and reselling materials, it selectively manufactures products where greater control over production can improve quality, supply and margins.
In metals, the FY26 annual report identifies six of 26 products manufactured in-house under brands including Noble, Bison and Sangam Steel, with more than 1.1 Mn tonnes of annual capacity.
It also reports that structural-steel capacity expanded from 100,000 to 500,000 tonnes a year.
Chemicals follow the same logic.

The FY26 report identifies in-house manufacturing for eight of 26 chemical products, with annual capacity exceeding 80,000 tonnes, and an expansion in ethyl acetate capacity from 10,000 to 80,000 tonnes.
The aim is to capture more value from selected products without abandoning the broader trading catalogue.
The strategy is selective rather than a complete shift away from trading.
In a September 2026 update, the company described manufacturing capabilities across more than 40 products and plans to expand into herbicides and pesticides.
The economics are improving, even as sales contract.
Commerce revenue fell 9.7% to ₹19,056 Cr in FY26, but its reported segment result excluding other income rose from ₹303 Cr to ₹527 Cr.
In his shareholder letter, cofounder Asish Mohapatra separately reported commerce EBITDA of ₹769 Cr, up 37.9%.
The two measures are not interchangeable, and neither reveals manufacturing’s standalone margin.
What they do establish is that commerce earnings improved despite lower revenue.
The question is whether this improvement can continue as the business invests in capacity, rather than relying on commodity-price recovery or portfolio exits.
If metals are OfBusiness’ biggest revenue generator, fashion and apparel is becoming its fastest-growing category.
The segment, which includes apparel, footwear and accessories, saw its revenue surge 141% from ₹1,171 Cr in FY25 to ₹2,828 Cr in FY26, more than doubling in a year.
Interestingly, of the where ₹1,171 Cr segment revenue in FY25, INR 376 Cr was apparel alone.
Unlike its traditional raw-material business, OfBusiness’ apparel operations focus on supplying finished products to global brands.
It works with smaller manufacturers, manages product development, quality approvals and production, and handles everything from order fulfilment to international deliveries.
As of March 2026, OfBusiness had developed capabilities to serve over 70 brands, including Michael Kors, Uniqlo, Adidas, IKEA, GAP and Zara.
Its apparel operations spanned 21 processing facilities, with annual in-house manufacturing capacity exceeding 40 Mn units.
Acquisitions have played a major role in OfBusiness’ apparel expansion.

It acquired footwear manufacturer Alpine Shoes in October 2024, followed by Bengaluru-based garment and home-textile exporter Indian Designs Exports in FY26, which became wholly owned in January 2026.
The acquisitions have broadened the product range and manufacturing footprint, but the report does not separate acquired growth from organic growth.
